target.name: obsolete mitochondrion-endoplasmic reticulum membrane tethering
target.description: Mitochondria and the endoplasmic reticulum are held in close apposition at contact sites, and the tethers that bridge the two membranes set how much calcium and lipid passes between them. These junctions matter because ER-released calcium taken up locally by mitochondria stimulates oxidative metabolism, while excessive transfer triggers permeability transition and apoptosis; contact spacing also influences mitochondrial division and autophagosome formation.

target.name: intracellular transport
target.description: Moving proteins, membranes and cargo between compartments is the logistical backbone of a eukaryotic cell, and intracellular transport covers the steps by which newly made proteins enter the secretory pathway, vesicles bud and fuse, endosomes mature, and macromolecules cross the nuclear envelope. Without it, secretion and receptor turnover fail and misfolded protein accumulates.

target.name: columnar/cuboidal epithelial cell maturation
target.description: Columnar and cuboidal epithelia line the gut, airway, kidney tubules and glands, and a newly specified cell of this shape must still acquire the transporters, junctions and secretory apparatus that make the sheet functional. This maturation step is distinct from the morphogenetic change that gives the cell its column or cube shape; it is the final differentiation that confers barrier and absorptive competence, and when it fails the epithelium remains immature, leaky or poorly polarised.

[untitled BTM module] Intestinal crypt epithelium maintained by Wnt signalling is what these genes describe: a stem and progenitor programme of the colonic crypt base together with markers of the differentiating epithelium above it. It sustains the continuous renewal of the gut lining, and its inappropriate reactivation underlies colorectal adenoma and carcinoma, where the same transcripts serve as tumour markers.

[untitled BTM module] These genes mark the differentiated absorptive and secretory epithelium of the gastrointestinal tract, the barrier layer that absorbs nutrients, detoxifies luminal xenobiotics and presents a glycan-coated surface to the microbiota. Adhesion and junctional components such as EPCAM and FERMT1 hold the sheet together, while lineage transcription factors including FOXA3 and KLF5 drive and maintain the differentiated state; loss of these programmes underlies barrier failure, inflammatory bowel disease and the dedifferentiation seen in colorectal cancer, where CEACAM and galectin-4 expression is routinely used as an epithelial marker.

[untitled BTM module] These genes outline the transcriptional and structural programme that gives absorptive epithelium of the gut and kidney tubule its identity: a polarized brush-border cell that moves solutes across a sealed barrier. HNF4G, TFAP2C and SIX4 act as lineage-directing transcription factors, while CLDN2 builds a cation- and water-permeable tight junction pore that sets paracellular leakiness, and SLC3A1 supplies the heavy subunit of the transporter that reabsorbs cystine and dibasic amino acids — its loss causes cystinuria with kidney stones.

[untitled BTM module] These genes mark the epithelial identity programme of stratified and glandular epithelia, particularly of the gastrointestinal tract, and its coordinated regulation of differentiation, adhesion and mucosal barrier function. Transcription factors set the programme: CDX1 specifies intestinal identity and is a determinant of intestinal metaplasia when expressed in stomach or oesophagus, while KLF5 and the ETS factor EHF drive proliferation and maturation of epithelial progenitors.

[untitled BTM module] These genes define the differentiated intestinal epithelium, the absorptive lineage that lines the small bowel and colon and carries out nutrient uptake, barrier maintenance and fluid balance. The programme is set by a transcription factor core in which CDX1 and CDX2 specify intestinal identity and HNF4A and HNF4G drive enterocyte maturation; loss or ectopic activation of these factors underlies intestinal metaplasia and is used to distinguish gut-derived tumours.

[untitled BTM module] This grouping describes the differentiated absorptive epithelium of the intestine and liver, the tissue that takes up nutrients, forms a selective barrier, and performs first-pass metabolism of drugs and dietary xenobiotics. Its identity is set transcriptionally by the nuclear receptors HNF4A and HNF4G, which drive expression of brush border and apical junction components such as villin, CDHR5 and the harmonin scaffold USH1C, together with the lectin LGALS4 and the tetraspanin-like TM4SF5.

[untitled BTM module] These genes mark the differentiated intestinal and hepatic epithelium and the transcriptional programme that specifies it. HNF4A and HNF4G, with FOXA3, act as master regulators of enterocyte and hepatocyte identity, driving expression of the brush-border and junctional machinery that makes an absorptive epithelium possible: villin as the microvillar actin-bundling protein, claudin-2 setting paracellular cation and water permeability in the proximal intestine, and harmonin (USH1C) organising apical scaffolds.

[untitled BTM module] These genes together mark the differentiated absorptive epithelium of the intestine, the cell layer that takes up nutrients, senses dietary and xenobiotic chemicals, and forms a barrier to gut contents. Lineage-defining transcription factors such as CDX1 and HNF4G impose regional intestinal identity on gut endoderm and drive expression of the enterocyte's working machinery: a brush border built with the unconventional myosin MYO1A, apical solute carriers including SLC3A1 for cystine and dibasic amino acids and the zinc transporter SLC39A5, and HMGCS2 for ketogenesis from fatty acids in a tissue with high energetic turnover.

target.name: nuclear pore complex
target.description: Every molecule that moves between nucleus and cytoplasm passes through the nuclear pore complex, the channel embedded in the nuclear envelope that both permits transport of RNA and proteins and enforces the compartment boundary that makes nuclear regulation possible. The listed nucleoporins fall into recognizable modules: the Y-shaped scaffold ring built from NUP107, NUP133, NUP160, NUP85, SEH1L and NUP37 anchors the structure to the membrane, while phenylalanine-glycine repeat proteins such as NUP62 and NUP54 line the central channel and create the selective permeability barrier.

target.name: DNA double-strand break processing
target.description: When both strands of DNA break, a cell must decide how to mend them, and the nucleolytic chewing back of the 5' strands is the step that commits the break to homologous recombination rather than end joining. The resulting 3' single-stranded tail is what RAD51 and its mediators coat to search for a sister chromatid template, so this processing determines repair fidelity and, with it, genome stability, chromosome integrity and resistance to radiation and crosslinking agents.

target.description: The outermost layer of skin keeps water in and pathogens out by means of lipid lamellae packed between corneocytes, and loading those lipids into lamellar granules depends on the keratinocyte transporter ABCA12. Adhesion and junctional components such as EPCAM and FERMT1 hold the sheet together, while lineage transcription factors including FOXA3 and KLF5 drive and maintain the differentiated state; loss of these programmes underlies barrier failure, inflammatory bowel disease and the dedifferentiation seen in colorectal cancer, where CEACAM and galectin-4 expression is routinely used as an epithelial marker.
